extracted.intended_audience: press release writers and communications professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing press releases that follow Associated Press (AP) style, covering structure, punctuation, capitalization, numbers, datelines, quotes, fonts, and other conventions to improve journalist acceptance and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper press release includes a headline, dateline, introductory paragraph, body paragraphs, quotes, boilerplate and media contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An AP-style press release should typically be between 300 and 500 words. Ensure all standard elements (headline, dateline, lead, body, quote(s), boilerplate, media contact) are present and clearly separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence case: capitalize only the first word and any proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid all-caps headlines. Use active voice and strong verbs to make the headline clear and newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Datelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Format: CITY, State (Month Day, Year) — followed by content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write cities in all caps. Use AP state abbreviations. Major cities (e.g., NEW YORK, LOS ANGELES) stand alone without the state. Place the dateline at the start of the first paragraph and follow the AP punctuation/spacing conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out one through nine; use numerals for 10 and above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerals always for ages, percentages, money, and dates. Apply AP number rules consistently throughout the release to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Months
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out month names when used alone; abbreviate when used with specific dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full month name (March) when alone; abbreviate with specific dates (March 5). AP abbreviations: Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec. May, June and July are never abbreviated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize job titles when they precede a name; lowercase when they follow a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: President John Smith (capitalize before). John Smith, president of Acme (lowercase after). Apply this consistently for clarity and AP compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Always attribute quotes with 'said' rather than alternatives like 'stated' or 'noted'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double quotation marks (single only for quotations within quotations). Introduce speakers with full name and title to establish credibility and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow AP punctuation norms: no Oxford/serial comma; one space after periods; avoid exclamation points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid punctuation that reads as informal or promotional. The no-Oxford-comma rule affects lists; use single spacing after sentence-ending periods per AP style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out an organization or term on first use with the abbreviation in parentheses, then use the abbreviation thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: American Medical Association (AMA), then 'AMA' for subsequent references. Do not rely on acronyms without establishing them first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use common readable fonts and appropriate point sizes for body and headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended fonts: Times New Roman, Arial, Calibri. Body text: 10-12 pt; headlines: 14-16 pt. Keep formatting simple and professional to ease newsroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and journalist acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases that follow AP style require less editing and signal professionalism to journalists and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists will notice style errors, which can detract from your message or lead them to dismiss the release entirely. Adhering to AP conventions increases the likelihood of pickup and reduces editorial friction.
